subjects.question: Who is looking at whom?
subjects.summary: An Edo carver made Portuguese figures support a container for salt. That combination joins skilled making, court institutions and a distant audience. Benin City, in present-day Nigeria, was the center of an existing kingdom, rather than a workshop waiting for European direction. The selected object’s broad date does not date the kingdom’s beginnings or identify a particular commission.

sections.title: Look at the work supporting the bowl
sections.text: In the supplied photograph, a standing figure faces outward below the container. Patterned clothing, beads, a cross and a long weapon organize the surface; other figures turn around its sides. Carving a freestanding support and a vessel from ivory required planning around the material. The museum describes four figures around the whole object. This single view does not show every side equally. A reader can compare visible detail with a catalogue claim without pretending the photograph is a complete inspection.

sections.title: A court sustained specialized production
sections.text: National Museums Scotland describes palace-controlled craft guilds producing objects for the Oba and court ceremonies. This institutional setting matters: makers learned and practiced within relationships of authority, patronage and access to materials. Court art supported succession and remembrance as well as display. Those functions do not make every surviving ivory a royal altar object. This saltcellar is associated with an export market; the catalogue qualifies its attribution to the court of Benin with a question mark.

sections.title: A customer’s request still needed a maker’s decisions
sections.text: The Met’s ivory essay describes commissions and imported models alongside local carving traditions and training. A European customer might recognize clothing, Christian signs or a table vessel while an Edo maker decided how bodies, supports and textured surfaces worked together. The name “Master of the Heraldic Ship” is a modern attribution, not a recovered signature. Recognizing an audience therefore does not recover the customer’s instructions, the carver’s biography or the payment for this object.

sections.title: Exchange changed the court’s material possibilities
sections.text: Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century contacts brought traded cloth, coral and brass into Benin’s wider court economy. These materials could become meaningful in local regalia rather than keeping one fixed foreign meaning. The saltcellar instead uses ivory to picture outsiders. Together, these examples show selection and transformation in different directions. They do not establish that every negotiation was equal or that all members of society benefited. A patron’s desirable object is only one outcome of the relationships that sustained production.

deeperReading.title: Follow an attribution without turning it into a person
deeperReading.text: A conventional master name groups works through similarities that an art historian considers significant. It can help compare carving choices while leaving the maker’s actual name, assistants and workshop organization unresolved. The saltcellar’s catalogue range, about 1525–1600, is broad enough to frustrate a story about one meeting with a named visitor. Its retained media search envelope begins at 1520; that numeric envelope is not a newly discovered exact date. A useful account keeps both the qualified attribution and the catalogue wording visible.

deeperReading.title: Distinguish an export object from a later collection event
deeperReading.text: Many export ivories reached European collections in early modern exchange. Separately, British forces invaded Benin in 1897, deposed its Oba and removed court belongings. The latter history is essential to understanding Benin collections, but it cannot establish this saltcellar’s custody without object-specific documentation. Its 1972 museum accession is a modern collection event, not its manufacture or proof of its earlier route. The consulted main catalogue view does not supply a complete provenance chain.

deeperReading.title: Bring missing work into the question
deeperReading.text: Ask how ivory was obtained, who learned the craft, who carried commissions and who received payment. These questions extend the account beyond a ruler and a foreign customer. The photograph cannot answer them by itself. Workshop, commercial and Edo historical evidence would help connect the finished carving to people’s choices and constraints. For example, an instruction might specify an intended design, while a payment record might reveal a different part of the relationship. Neither would substitute for the maker’s own account.

subjects.question: How far can a fragment take us?
subjects.summary: Silver and manufactured goods crossed the Pacific through a system supported by skilled and coerced work. One wreck, colonial shipbuilding reports and a later Mexican jar make different parts of that history concrete. Their contexts explain some connections while leaving particular makers, labor experiences and object journeys unresolved.

sections.title: Moving goods required several kinds of work
sections.text: The Manila trade joined American silver with Asian manufactured goods, including porcelain and silk. Hecht describes transfers through the Philippines and Acapulco, with some goods staying in the Americas and others crossing Mexico for onward shipment. This was a system of transactions and transport, not a single journey made by every object. Ships also required prepared timber and metalwork. Pineda’s report names people cutting and planing wood, shaping masts and forging nails: useful skills without which a trading connection could not remain afloat.

sections.title: Royal construction placed burdens on communities
sections.text: In 1618 Governor Fajardo reported that royal shipbuilding drew people away from their fields. He described harsh work and contributions from neighbors to support workers whose royal pay was small. Pineda’s separately attributed 1619 report lists different skilled tasks, then describes arrears and people leaving. A stated wage was not necessarily money received. These officials sought changes that would sustain royal service and reduce expense. Their accounts expose burdens without supplying the workers’ own full testimony or establishing identical conditions in every yard and year.

sections.title: Follow one interrupted voyage
sections.text: The San Agustín carried Chinese goods from the Philippines toward Mexico in 1595. It wrecked at tamál-húye, present-day Drakes Bay, where Coast Miwok communities already lived. Porcelain recovered in village contexts gives this episode a material setting beyond a captain’s account. The NPS project compares excavation records and written sources while investigating how local people selected and used introduced objects. Proposed practical and ceremonial uses remain interpretations to test, rather than one meaning assigned to every fragment.

deeperReading.title: An official’s criticism has a purpose
deeperReading.text: Fajardo contrasts royal construction with smaller private ships, whose workers he describes as paid and consenting. His proposed permission concerns regional navigation, not proof that all Pacific galleon building was voluntary. He also considers buying enslaved people elsewhere for galley service. Criticism of one damaging arrangement therefore does not make the letter a program of freedom for everyone. Pineda similarly writes to the king about preserving the colony and improving royal provision. His technical knowledge and complaints help explain work while leaving the workers’ different aims harder to recover. Both accounts are read here through an old English edition, without an independent check of their Spanish manuscripts.

subjects.question: What happens when a story meets a new language and audience?
subjects.summary: Making an illustrated book joined translation, writing, painting and patronage. Akbar’s court gathered specialists with different languages and artistic training. In the selected Harivamsa folio, Krishna shelters villagers beneath a mountain. The page connects a sacred narrative with a late-sixteenth-century imperial book project; it does not describe every reader, maker or religious community.

sections.title: A composition makes the story visible
sections.text: In the painting, the mountain forms a broad canopy above a central figure with a raised arm. People and cattle gather below, while rocky slopes and animals fill the upper field. The museum identifies Krishna protecting the villagers of Braj from Indra’s rain. Choosing where bodies, rocks and shelter fit was part of making the narrative visible. This is an illustrated sacred story, made around 1590–95, rather than an eyewitness record of that event.

sections.title: Different skills made a book possible
sections.text: Bookmaking brought several kinds of skilled work together. The V&A describes the House of Books as both a library and a place of manuscript production, with painters, calligraphers, illuminators and binders. Persian translations made Sanskrit works available in the court’s literary language. The British Library’s record for another manuscript names Naqib Khan as translator of the Mahabharata into Persian. Translation, writing and image-making were related tasks; they were not necessarily performed by a single author or painter.

sections.title: Language and patronage shaped an audience
sections.text: A Persian book could address readers who did not know the original language. The V&A explains this change of audience through the Persian translation of Babur’s Turki memoirs, alongside translations of Sanskrit works. Commissions also presented the ruler as a source of knowledge. Historian Christian Blake Pye reads Abu al-Fazl’s 1587 Razmnama preface as joining religious inquiry with Akbar’s imperial authority. Bringing traditions into a court project therefore involved political choices, alongside intellectual curiosity and artistic work.

sections.title: Teams and patrons changed
sections.text: Some manuscript margins preserve working attributions. Yael Rice’s research abstract distinguishes designers and colourists, and argues that changing teams helped produce an imperial style across selected projects. That supplies a mechanism for collaboration beyond calling a page beautiful. Patronage also continued after Akbar: a separate Razmnama folio dated 1616–17 was made for the commander Abd al-Rahim. Different commissions could bring familiar stories to further courtly settings without making this selected leaf evidence for everyone’s religious life.

deeperReading.title: A preface has a speaker and a purpose
deeperReading.text: Pye interprets taḥqīq in Abu al-Fazl’s preface as an inquiry into or realization of religious truth, connected to a Sufi intellectual tradition and the emperor’s authority. This is a scholar’s reading of an elite argument, not modern laboratory verification or a measurement of popular agreement. Pye also notes that later peace terminology was applied retroactively. A translated preface can illuminate how power was justified without proving that each subject enjoyed equal power or understood the project alike.

deeperReading.title: Copies reach us through different histories
deeperReading.text: The British Library describes dispersed Razmnama leaves around 1598 and a surviving final volume catalogued separately. Its records identify a later copy, not the first commission. The catalogue’s attribution to Naqib Khan concerns textual translation; it does not name the painter of the supplied Harivamsa leaf. Digital manuscript images are currently unavailable, so no colophon reading is claimed here. Such gaps change what can be checked, even when the catalogue remains informative.

subjects.question: Whose account survives when trade becomes conquest?
subjects.summary: Banda’s spice commerce depended on cultivation, skilled processing and imported food. The VOC’s campaign imposed monopoly through killing, enslavement and displacement. Colonial records expose policy; continuing Bandanese communities and attributed modern voices show why the story cannot end with the company’s claim to control.

sections.title: Spice commerce supported a society
sections.text: Nutmeg and mace were products of work and exchange before the VOC sought to monopolize them. The National Archives account explains that Bandanese commerce brought food as well as income: much food came from outside the islands. It describes orang kaya as merchants with political authority, whose important decisions involved discussion with villagers. Mostert and Manuhutu describe Dutch visitors in 1599 paying port dues and exchanging goods in an existing trading society. Exclusive buying rights threatened relationships on which people’s living depended.

citations.locator: Opening: trade and first Dutch visit

sections.title: A monopoly claim became control over food and place
sections.text: A contract did not automatically stop people trading with other buyers. Forts and military force became means of imposing company claims. In 1621 the VOC council ordered people removed from Banda Besar; Coen’s report discusses using hunger against those resisting in the hills. The archive presents these policies within an account of genocide. The decisions connect commerce with access to food, homes and freedom. An official report makes those purposes legible while leaving the people targeted far less able to explain themselves in the same collection.

sections.title: Plantation production depended on people’s knowledge
sections.text: After the conquest, the company allocated land to colonial settlers and organized production through perken, or plantation plots. The archive’s account distinguishes settlers who received land from the enslaved people compelled to cultivate it. Enslaved people brought from several regions worked them. Bandanese survivors were also forced to cultivate and transfer knowledge about the trees; this was not an empty landscape awaiting productive newcomers. Cultivation and processing still required expertise. Mostert and Manuhutu trace further persecution after 1621, but also communities in Seram, Makassar and Kei maintaining relationships and political initiatives. Forced displacement changed society without ending Bandanese lives or making the company’s claim to complete control reliable.

sections.title: Living people continue to interpret the past
sections.text: In a public statement dated 8 May 2021, named representatives identifying themselves as Wandan descendants in Banda Ely-Elat connected ancestral dispossession with a protest against Coen’s commemoration in Hoorn. Their words are evidence of their present claim, not every community’s single opinion. Muhammad Farid, a Banda-based educator, separately argues that remembrance should support honest historical writing and protection of Banda’s future. These are people addressing audiences and seeking consequences. Reading them alongside the company’s account changes whose purposes a history must explain.

deeperReading.title: Different records make different kinds of claims
deeperReading.text: The National Archives explicitly warns that its Banda collection, as known to the institution, does not contain Bandanese voices. A council decision can establish what officials advised without becoming a family’s testimony of removal. Likewise, a modern protest is not an eyewitness account of 1621. It makes a different historical fact accessible: named descendants publicly contest how their ancestors and a colonial governor are remembered. Farid’s proposal to contextualize colonial symbols and the statement’s opposition to a public statue need not be flattened into agreement. Identify each speaker, date, audience and purpose before asking where their accounts meet or differ.

deeperReading.title: Continuity does not give unrestricted access
deeperReading.text: Faradika Darman, writing for the Maluku language office, distinguishes everyday language from ritual language and describes the role of people entrusted to perform Kabata. The article also states that some ritual material must not be documented. A fuller history should respect that limit instead of treating every living tradition as freely extractable classroom content. This account therefore does not reproduce or ask families to perform sacred songs. Publicly offered statements can be read on their own terms while unconsulted or restricted knowledge remains outside the account. The three island markers have a similarly bounded purpose: modern published coordinates orient names, but do not recover a village household, a path of flight or anyone’s cultural authority.

evidenceReading.title: Policy, consequence and a living public claim
evidenceReading.introduction: These source capsules are editorial paraphrases. Their dates and purposes remain different; no graphic passage, ritual text or precise casualty estimate is reproduced.

items.label: An order exposes a policy, not every experience
items.text: The archive transcribes the council’s 24 April 1621 advice to remove named communities and presents Coen’s 6 May report about forcing opponents out through hunger.
items.interpretation: The record supports a conclusion about official intentions and the means proposed. It does not prove that every instruction occurred exactly as written or provide the households’ own testimony. The archive identifies that imbalance in its collection.

items.label: A claim of control does not erase continuing communities
items.text: The PALA account contrasts colonial claims of near-total destruction with later records of Bandanese people maintaining communities, trade and political contacts outside the islands.
items.interpretation: Following later evidence changes a story that would end in 1621. It establishes continuing activity without tracing each family’s migration, settling one population total or reconstructing a universal route.

items.label: A dated public statement is a modern source in its own right
items.text: The 8 May 2021 authors identify themselves as descendants of Wandan living in Banda Ely-Elat and address a protest to Hoorn about the public commemoration of Coen.
items.interpretation: This is evidence of these signatories’ self-identification, grievances and intended audience. Their voice need not stand for every Bandanese person, and their historical estimates are not adopted as a verified census. Reading a public statement does not confer permission to copy restricted traditions or claim community approval.

familyActivity.title: Two dates, two purposes and a careful conclusion
steps: Read the two source capsules with an adult. Put 1621 and 2021 on separate cards; do not turn the distance between them into a claim that nothing happened in between.

For each card, name the speaker and decision or change being sought. Identify the intended audience when the capsule gives it; otherwise mark that as an unanswered question. Point to the words supporting each answer.
Use the three island-reference labels to distinguish Banda Besar, Neira and Rhun. Explain why these points cannot show a particular family’s journey or a battle.
Write one supported claim and one question that would require another freely offered source. Do not invent a victim’s diary, reenact violence or perform a sacred song.

These are colonial officials’ records. In a separate public statement dated 8 May 2021, named Banda Ely-Elat representatives identifying themselves as Wandan descendants addressed Hoorn’s municipal authorities to protest Coen’s public commemoration. The later statement makes its authors’ living claim visible. It is not a 1621 eyewitness report or proof of every community’s opinion. The activity asks about purpose and evidence, without graphic detail or restricted ritual material.

subjects.name: Haiti: freedom fought for in a plantation world
subjects.geographicPrecision: Gonaïves declaration-region locator; the revolution involved many places and changing alliances.

interval.label: Revolutionary investigation, 1791–1804
interval.note: Uprising to independence; not the end of the consequences of slavery or colonial power.

subjects.question: Who made freedom, and why was it contested?
subjects.summary: Enslaved people’s resistance broke the plantation order, but emancipation, control of work and independence were distinct struggles. Regional research, a leader’s letter and constitutional rules show people making different political choices. The 1804 declaration severed French rule while also establishing authority; it does not speak directly for every household.

sections.title: Resistance grew through different local struggles
sections.text: Sugar and coffee production depended on coerced work. In 1791, enslaved people challenged that order in the northern plantation region. Sabine Manigat’s research distinguishes this uprising from different conflicts in the West and South. Insurgent groups, free people of color, colonists and competing armies formed shifting alliances rather than one stable camp. War and negotiation created openings for people seeking liberty. Regional differences help explain how a struggle could change direction without assuming everyone began with the same plan for an independent nation.

sections.title: Emancipation had to be defended and interpreted
sections.text: Provincial emancipation measures in 1793 preceded the French Convention’s 1794 colonial abolition decree. Deputies carried events in Saint-Domingue into metropolitan politics. Louverture, a formerly enslaved leader, offers one particular political voice. His 1797 letter asks Vincent to defend him before the Directory, rejects racist accusations and affirms attachment to France. The argument makes sense within that moment’s commitments. It does not turn him into the spokesman for every cultivator, nor make independence the inevitable meaning of all earlier resistance.

citations.locator: Le débat: provincial measures, delegation and decree

sections.title: Ending slavery did not settle control of work
sections.text: The 1801 constitution prohibits slavery and calls people free and French. It also insists that cultivation continue. Articles 15–16 picture an estate as a family led by its owner or representative, promise cultivators a share of revenues and treat changes of residence as a threat to production. The governor receives police powers to regulate them. This language connects agricultural output with political control: freedom from enslavement and freedom to leave a workplace were not treated as identical questions. The rules are evidence of a governing project, not proof that workers consented or received what was promised.

sections.title: Independence created another political settlement
sections.text: The French expedition of 1802 renewed the threat to emancipation and met resistance. Independence was proclaimed in 1804. The Acte records assembled generals renouncing France; its claim of agreement concerns that gathering. Armitage and Gaffield distinguish the official printed pamphlet and broadside from a lost manuscript stage. They also identify an accompanying oath making Dessalines governor general for life. Political separation and the defense of liberty therefore came with a new concentration of authority. Other records are needed for landholding, work and participation beyond the leaders’ declarations.

deeperReading.title: A signature, a scribe and a printed name do different work
deeperReading.text: The Smithsonian distinguishes the unidentified writer of the 1797 letter from Louverture’s signature. Its volunteer transcription contains uncertain readings, so the account paraphrases clear passages rather than claiming a complete critical translation. The museum’s brief independence-threat caption is not adopted as this letter’s verified wording. The 1804 document is a different object history: scholarship describes government printing, transmission and authorization. A name reproduced in print is not an autograph, and a printed proclamation is not a verbatim transcript of every speech at Gonaïves.

deeperReading.title: A constitution supplies a project, not a complete outcome
deeperReading.text: Reading abolition beside cultivation rules exposes a concrete tension. The 1801 text promises a revenue share while restricting movement and assigning the governor enforcement powers. It does not supply each worker’s income, complaint, negotiation or response. Calling the estate a family is a governing metaphor, not evidence of kinship or voluntary agreement. Manigat’s regional account likewise warns against making one group’s situation stand for the whole colony. A fuller investigation needs cultivators’ and women’s accounts, local enforcement records and household evidence. Independence in 1804 did not make those questions disappear; this packet does not extend them into unverified 1825 financial claims.

deeperReading.title: Read political changes forward through time
deeperReading.text: Read the 1797 letter beside article 1 of the 1801 constitution and the 1804 oath. These records first join freedom with French allegiance, then mark a political separation. They do not establish one unchanging intention for every participant. Explaining that change requires the circumstances of each record, rather than assigning the final outcome backward to 1791.

evidenceReading.title: Political voices, work rules and a circulated act
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of French transcriptions and selected scholarship. They are not new critical translations, unmediated access to every enslaved voice or a collation of the original 1804 pamphlet.

items.label: A leader’s letter is an argument to a recipient
items.text: The 1797 Vincent letter seeks advocacy with the French Directory, contests racist allegations and affirms attachment to France.
items.interpretation: It supplies a particular political position at that date. It is not the later Directory letter, a universal statement of formerly enslaved people’s views or evidence that independence was every insurgent’s fixed objective in 1791.

items.label: An abolition clause coexists with work regulation
items.text: Article 3 of the 1801 constitution prohibits slavery; articles 14–16 protect continuing cultivation and empower regulation of cultivators’ movement.
items.interpretation: The combination reveals a governing project and a tension within freedom. It does not establish consent, actual payments or identical enforcement on every estate.

items.label: The act’s recorded agreement has a defined group
items.text: The modern French transcription identifies assembled generals as swearing the 1804 independence oath. Scholarship separately describes the official printed packet.
items.interpretation: Recorded unanimity in that assembly does not establish a population-wide vote. The printed version, manuscript copies, modern transcription and lost manuscript stage must not be treated as one physical object.

interval.note: A bounded investigation of sixteenth-century work, seventeenth-century markets and eighteenth-century building, ending with the cited 1748–55 mosque example. These are not the Ottoman Empire’s founding or dissolution dates.

subjects.question: How did skilled work serve both public authority and people buying things?
subjects.summary: A tughra, a painted dish and workshop remains reveal different kinds of skilled work. Named decorators, material study and accounts of commissions and markets connect production with people while keeping the particular maker and buyer of an unsigned object unknown.

sections.title: Writing through shared tasks
sections.text: An official emblem could require more than one pair of hands. The Met distinguishes the specialist who drew a tughra’s standard form from an illuminator who decorated certain imperial documents. In the selected example, tall shafts, loops and blue-and-gold ornament organize the paper surface. The writing represents Süleyman’s authority through names, titles and a claim of victory. It is work performed for a ruler, rather than proof that he drew every emblem himself or that everyone receiving a document could read it.

sections.title: Making a ceramic surface
sections.text: The round Iznik dish joins a formed body, painted design and transparent glazed surface. Stonepaste is a prepared ceramic material, rather than Chinese porcelain. The museum dates this vessel around 1575–90 and describes a local design language that adapted admired Chinese examples. A study of other Iznik samples identified different glasses used to prepare their bodies. Choosing and combining materials helped makers obtain a body suitable for a finished vessel. Makers arranged plants and birds within a bounded circular field. Preparing a usable material and fitting decoration to a shape were different problems. Neither the pattern nor the catalogue identifies this dish’s particular workshop, buyer or original meal.

sections.title: Names and production remains
sections.text: Other objects and excavations make workers’ tasks more visible. A separate British Museum lamp bears a date equivalent to 1549 and names Musli as its decorator. That is evidence about this lamp, not a signature on the selected dish. Excavation authors at Iznik report firing equipment, defective pieces and semi-finished tiles. Such remains connect finished-looking designs with preparation, firing and things that went wrong. Comparisons with tiles in seventeenth-century buildings help investigate production and dating without supplying a complete roster of makers.

sections.title: Work for patrons and buyers
sections.text: Court commissions were one source of work among others. An Ashmolean course excerpts John Covel’s 1670s description of a weekly market and ceramic materials. Sardar’s later synthesis explains how fixed court payments could make open-market work more attractive. These are attributed accounts, not every workshop’s balance sheet. Religious foundations and urban building also required continuing production and upkeep. Eighteenth-century patrons commissioned new works, including the 1748–55 Nur-u Osmaniye Mosque. Keeping these settings distinct explains changing opportunities without making all ceramics market goods or all writing palace labor.

deeperReading.title: A material study is not a workshop recipe book
deeperReading.text: Paynter and colleagues examined pottery and tile samples with associated glass and used laboratory replicas to investigate their interpretation. Their abstract distinguishes body and glaze compositions and reports separate glasses in the studied stonepaste bodies. This makes material selection an active part of skilled production. It does not identify the complete recipe, fuel, firing schedule or supplier of the selected Met dish. A chemical result can support a manufacturing explanation while leaving wages, ownership and division of labor unresolved.

deeperReading.title: A market account has a speaker
deeperReading.text: Covel’s description reaches this inquiry through Rosser-Owen’s teaching-course excerpt, rather than a freshly read manuscript. It records a visitor’s market and material observations. His comparative judgments do not measure the experience of every potter. Sardar’s court-payment explanation is a separate modern synthesis; it does not replace workshop accounts or direct reading of the cited edicts. A signature, archaeological residue and economic account answer related questions through different evidence.

deeperReading.title: Dates belong to different records

subjects.name: Isfahan and New Julfa: silk, city and forced movement
subjects.geographicPrecision: City locator; New Julfa lies south of the river. Carpet workshops were also in Yazd and Kashan; an individual carpet is not securely assigned to this point.

interval.label: Selected Safavid capital phase, 1597–98 to 1722
interval.note: Start follows the conventional 1597–98 capital transfer, plotted at 1598. The endpoint marks the selected capital phase, not Isfahan’s existence or every later Safavid dynastic claim.

subjects.question: Who made a prosperous capital—and whose movement was coerced?
subjects.summary: Isfahan’s prosperity joined urban building, rural silk, skilled making, commerce and household work. New Julfa’s institutions developed after forced relocation. The carpet, merchant correspondence and a later family letter make different relationships visible without identifying one common experience, a particular weaver or a route for this object.

sections.title: A new centre within an older city
sections.text: Isfahan did not begin with the conventional capital transfer of 1597–98. Haneda and Matthee describe gradual development and a mobile royal household. A new governmental and commercial centre grew southwest of the older one. Shops, caravansaries, bathhouses and coffeehouses gathered around the royal square and adjacent bazaar; the older centre remained important. A bazaar entrance stood at the square’s north end. This relationship makes the square one connection within a larger city, rather than a picture of its entire economy. These named relationships explain how buying, lodging and service work shared urban space. New Julfa lay south of the Zayandarud, rather than inside every picture of the royal square.

citations.locator: Isfahan as the Safavid Capital: new commercial centre and urban quarters

sections.title: Silk connected several kinds of making
sections.text: Munroe distinguishes rural raw-silk producers, private urban workshops and court production. Dyers, weavers, embroiderers and designers contributed different skills. Repeated patterns required coordination between design and material work. The Met identifies the selected Doria carpet as silk pile with metal-wrapped thread, made with knotting and brocading. This is a particular carpet technique, not every cloth process in the essay. The type is associated with several Iranian centres, including Isfahan, Yazd and Kashan; its appearance cannot name the individual workshop or weavers.

sections.title: A prosperous quarter followed forced movement
sections.text: In 1604, state-directed destruction and deportation uprooted Armenians from Old Julfa. Settlement at New Julfa began in 1605. Ghougassian distinguishes mercantile deportees from other displaced people and identifies later movements of artisans. Houses, churches, craft and service work helped make the new community. Painters and metalworkers appear beside gardeners, porters and other laborers in the account. Privileges for some merchants and later commercial achievement do not turn coercion into voluntary migration or establish equal wealth and freedom within the quarter.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population; Society and administration

sections.title: Commerce required relationships and information
sections.text: Tajiryan’s study describes the Girach-Mirman brothers pooling funds in New Julfa in 1656. Their particular gem-trading business paired capital with travelling agents and correspondence. A translated 1700 letter about turquoise exposes disagreement over prices and the difficulty of obtaining goods. Negotiating and sharing information were work, alongside transporting or making things. This example does not document a silk transaction or the selected carpet’s journey. Reading it beside the urban and craft accounts adds practical coordination without reducing the city to a ruler’s building program.

deeperReading.title: A household could contain unequal dependencies
deeperReading.text: Ghougassian’s synthesis draws on fragmentary histories, colophons, letters and community records. Its particular seventeenth-century wills reveal houses, commercial holdings, servants and enslaved dependants; some grants of freedom were delayed until the owner’s death. These examples make dependence part of a prosperous community’s history. They do not supply an average household, establish that every servant was enslaved or make all residents wealthy merchants. The original wills were not independently consulted here. An account of collective institutions therefore needs questions about who controlled property and whose work sustained it.

deeperReading.title: A later family voice changes the question
deeperReading.text: The UCLA account presents Anna Khatoon’s letter from New Julfa to her husband, a textile merchant. Its supplied translation includes family greetings, a request for his safe return and an enclosed lock of hair. The rendered date, 9 August 1747, is later than the entire 1598–1722 case. This comparison brings separation and family communication into view without becoming testimony to the 1604 deportation. It is one mediated voice, not every woman’s experience. Together with commercial correspondence, it suggests that letters could carry different concerns within distant trade relationships. The original manuscript and Armenian translation were not independently checked, and the author’s hypotheses about literacy or the hair’s purpose remain hypotheses.

sections.title: A book made through several acts
sections.text: This folio joins writing, painted figures, patterned surfaces and gold on paper. The Met attributes its painting to Shaikh Zada. The manuscript was likely copied in Herat, then illustrated for an Uzbek patron, probably in Bukhara in the 1530s. Sa‘di’s poem, completed in 1257, was older than both acts. Words had to be copied and a painted scene arranged on a bounded page. Those tasks did not happen at the poem’s composition. The reception gives selected forms of luxury a place within a literary image; it does not supply a survey of ordinary homes.

sections.title: Skills moved, and workshops organized work
sections.text: Comstock-Skipp describes invited and captured artists contributing to manuscripts in sixteenth-century Bukhara. Movement could involve coercion as well as opportunity. She interprets repeated figures and compositions in later books as evidence of organized production, challenging the assumption that repetition simply means inferior art. A general material account adds practical tasks: smoothing paper and preparing pigment with a binder precede controlled brushwork. These help explain skilled making without identifying this folio’s complete staff, exact pigments or workshop recipe.

sections.title: Teaching used rooms that needed care
sections.text: Learning also depended on built places. The architectural account describes the older Ulugh Beg madrasa with a courtyard, cells, a classroom and a mosque. Built in 1417, it was restored in 1585. Learning and prayer thus depended on physical spaces within an institution whose fabric could be repaired. Mir-i Arab, dated 1535–36, added another foundation to the city. These descriptions make education more concrete than a list of famous monuments, while leaving daily timetables and the experience of particular students unresolved.

sections.title: Water and income sustained institutions
sections.text: Canals supplied fields, while drainage carried away runoff and helped manage salts. McChesney explains why construction, maintenance and investment mattered, with Bukhara examples in a wider regional account. Urban reservoirs belonged to this work of provision: the Lab-i Hauz complex brought a reservoir together with a madrasa and khanaqah in 1619–23. Endowed property supplied income for institutions and their employees. The wealthy Juybari family sponsored repairs, canals and learning foundations while also preserving family influence. Books and buildings therefore lead to people managing resources, not only the patrons whose names survive.

deeperReading.title: A foundation had records as well as walls
deeperReading.text: McChesney distinguishes purchase records, endowment deeds and biographies favorable to the Juybari family. They do different work as evidence. Property income could support public institutions, while establishing an endowment also helped perpetuate the family. His account of administrative roles includes scribes and supervision of household and workshop accounts. Such records bring calculation and supervision into view alongside monumental patronage. They do not make every employee’s voice equally audible. A biography praising its patron and a deed defining resources should not be treated as interchangeable descriptions of a shared experience. Here the original manuscripts and deeds remain unread; the explanation uses the historian’s selected analysis.

deeperReading.title: Maintenance also raises a question about power
deeperReading.text: A canal was not useful simply because someone once ordered it built. Continued water flow depended on maintenance and resources, and land value varied with access to the system. This practical relationship linked fields, food and urban institutions. It could also create unequal obligations. McChesney describes requisitioned labor in a large project in the Vakhsh basin. That example belongs to another location; it is not a recovered crew for Bukhara’s reservoir. It does show why useful infrastructure should not automatically be called voluntary cooperation. The present sources explain investment and institutional support more clearly than household water rights, everyday cleaning routines or the conditions of particular workers.

subjects.summary: A painted case joins practical storage with skilled surface work. Its flowers, birds, mirror and compartments invite close observation, while the museum supplies its maker, date and intended dressing function. A separately dated account of Shiraz connects building, merchants and artisans without turning an Iranian object into evidence for everyone’s life or a named ruler’s possessions.

A citadel, mosque, gardens and covered bazaar formed part of the building work. Merchants from Europe and India and artisans attracted from Isfahan contributed to the city’s activity. A favorable recollection by Abd al-Razzaq Donboli offers a particular observer’s later memory of the Shiraz court. Donboli had been a hostage and guest, and later wrote in a Qajar setting. subjects.summary: Mud preserved wooden household belongings at Ozette unusually well. Cedar working, food getting, storage and life in large houses can be investigated together. The burial chronology is disputed, and later photographs of Makah life are labeled as later evidence.

sections.title: Preservation changes what history can see
sections.text: The Makah museum describes a storm exposing wooden artifacts in 1969–70 and a collaborative excavation beginning in April 1970. Normally perishable material survived in the mud. A rich wooden assemblage can correct a picture dominated by stone tools, but survival is still selective. What was preserved beneath part of the village is not a complete inventory of everything used by every Makah household.

sections.text: The Tribe’s construction account describes hollowing cedar and steaming the sides rather than cutting away all their strength. Replaceable hardwood strips protected canoe sides found at Ozette. Navigation also relied on weather, swells and landmarks. Those are connected forms of expertise, not a choice between technology and knowledge. The account says sails were not found in the deposits; that absence does not securely date the invention or arrival of sails.

deeperReading.title: A material sequence is not a newly recovered scene
deeperReading.text: The Tribe’s public account explains how steam and wood grain connect: flaring softened sides avoids weakening them by cutting across the grain. It also names protective strips that could be replaced after paddling wear. These are reasons for choices and maintenance, rather than a picture of one recorded carver’s day. Only the gunwale statement is explicitly attached to Ozette finds in this passage. Neither the account nor the preserved later photograph supplies the dimensions, maker, work duration or full history of a particular excavated canoe.

deeperReading.title: Custody and permission are part of interpretation
deeperReading.text: The Makah museum presents the recovered collection through oral history and the Tribe’s desire to care for and interpret it. The museum connects the houses and household objects to a place Makah people remember and care for today. The setting and the age of the slide answer different questions. Researchers have proposed different calendar dates for the burial. A later photograph can show a canoe at the time the camera was used, while the excavated fittings carry evidence of earlier work.

evidenceReading.title: Shape, steam and replace: read a public material-work account
evidenceReading.introduction: These three editorial paraphrases form a material-work reading sequence. They use the Tribe’s public explanation, not a copied plan, new experiment or instruction to reproduce a cultural object.

items.label: Shape the cedar
items.text: The Tribe’s public account describes hollowing a red-cedar log. This stage removes material, but the desired final width was not obtained simply by carving away every part of the sides.
items.interpretation: Material removal is one part of making. The source’s account of construction should not be assigned automatically to every object or household.

items.label: Use heat to change the shape
items.text: Water and heated rocks supplied steam; the softened sides could be flared while retaining straight-grain strength. This explains a material decision in the account, not a measured procedure recovered from the later photograph.
items.interpretation: The reason for using heat concerns wood structure. No exact temperature, tool kit, timing or measured geometry is supplied here.

items.label: Protect a part that wears
items.text: The account identifies hardwood gunwales laced to canoe sides found at Ozette. These protective strips took wear from paddling and could be replaced. Maintenance belongs alongside initial making.
items.interpretation: This passage specifically connects a replaceable protective part with Ozette finds. It does not identify the later photograph’s boat as an excavated specimen.

subjects.question: How much coordinated work lies beyond the dramatic moment at the cliff?
subjects.summary: A communal bison hunt joined preparation, coordinated movement and the work of making food and materials usable. Blackfoot collaborative accounts connect the cliff with camp, fuel, water, drying and later hide work. This selected landscape and later historical window do not represent every Plains society or the beginning of bison knowledge.

sections.title: Preparation connected people, animals and a place
sections.text: The cliff was one part of a working landscape. UNESCO identifies drive lanes, bone deposits and processing camps as well as the escarpment. The Blackfoot/Glenbow collaborative exhibition explains why knowledge of bison behavior, wind and terrain mattered to preparation. A successful communal hunt depended on people acting together at the right moment. The material traces and public teaching account thus answer different parts of the same question: how a gathering of people could organize work across a much larger area than a photograph shows.

sections.title: Coordination mattered before the animals reached the edge
sections.text: The collaborative account describes runners and others placed along drive lanes. Timing mattered: revealing people too early could turn a herd away. The interpretive-site history also describes organizations that regulated camp movement and communal hunting. These sources make planning and coordination visible without assuming a permanent farming settlement was required for social institutions. Their descriptions are situated interpretations, not a roster of one hunt or a fixed constitution shared by every Blackfoot group in every year.

sections.title: Processing changed the pace and kinds of work
sections.text: After the hunt, work continued quickly at the camp. The exhibition explains cutting meat for drying, removing hides carefully and obtaining fat from bones. These activities needed water, fuel and equipment, linking the choice of campsite to practical demands. Hide preparation required more time than removing a hide and was not always completed during the communal hunt. Drying and storage extended the use of food beyond the immediate event. This sequence makes processing a central achievement rather than an invisible task after the dramatic moment.

Blackfoot Crossing describes bison providing clothing, shelter and tools as well as food, and trade conducted through protocols of respect. The sources also place these practical relations within spiritual responsibilities. Public descriptions help a reader understand that connection; they do not transfer authority to reproduce ceremonies. The c.1700–1850 case is a selected later inquiry. Much earlier archaeological use, later photographs and continuing community knowledge keep their own dates.

Brink’s chapter 7 adds another method: a grease-processing experiment involving Piikani crew member Hazel Big Smoke, cattle bones and modern tools. Those conditions matter when judging what the experiment tests. It is neither an ancient meal nor an exact reenactment. Likewise, a modern painting or a later photograph captioned on the teaching website cannot silently become an image of the selected 1700–1850 case. subjects.question: What changes when women’s gardens and houses are placed at the center of Plains history?
subjects.summary: Women’s gardens, houses and food stores helped make Hidatsa villages places of household work and regional exchange. Cultivation joined hunting and gathering rather than replacing them. Community-authored teaching and a named woman’s later recollections explain knowledge and authority while distinguishing Big Hidatsa from subsequent homes, displacement and continuing life.

sections.title: Gardens produced food and possibilities for exchange
sections.text: The community-authored NPS guide places women’s cultivation at the center of village economic life. Preparing land, tending corn, beans, squash and sunflowers, then drying and storing food required a connected sequence of work. Stored crops could sustain a household beyond harvest and supply exchange with visitors. Hunting and gathering also contributed to the food base. A village was therefore more than a cluster of buildings: fields, drying spaces and storage linked its residents to the surrounding land and other communities.

sections.title: An earthlodge joined construction with household authority
sections.text: NPS describes women constructing, owning and maintaining earthlodges through clan cooperation and experienced supervision. Gathering building material and making a supporting framework were practical tasks connected with knowledge and responsibility. Drying racks and cache pits extended this work into food storage. The standing interpretive lodge helps explain a structure, while shallow depressions mark former houses at Big Hidatsa. These are different forms of evidence. Neither the modern building nor the tool illustration establishes every historical resident, tool maker or ownership arrangement by appearance alone.

sections.title: The river brought visitors and changing pressures
sections.text: River travel helped make the villages places of exchange. Goods, visitors and disease moved through these relationships; the NPS historical account connects the 1837 smallpox epidemic with a steamboat arrival. MHA’s history describes village survivors consolidating and the 1845 move to Like-a-Fishhook. Such changes altered residence and community organization. The Big Hidatsa occupation frame ends at that move, not at the end of a people. The different Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara histories should be read together without erasing their distinctions.

sections.title: Later voices explain continuity through changed settings
sections.text: Maxi´diwiac, also known as Buffalobird-woman, describes garden boundaries, permission to use adjoining ground and letting fields rest in an account published in 1917. Her memories concern Like-a-Fishhook, after the selected Big Hidatsa occupation. They add a particular woman’s knowledge rather than a timeless rule for all earlier villages. Twentieth-century government projects brought further displacement. MHA’s account describes families moved from fertile bottomlands as the Garrison Dam transformed their landscape. That later history belongs to the separate reference, alongside the knowledge and communities that continued.

deeperReading.title: A named account still has an interpreter and editor
deeperReading.text: Wilson’s foreword describes recording Maxi´diwiac’s account through Edward Goodbird’s translation in 1912 and reading earlier notes back for corrections during later visits. He also explains arranging the material and its English idiom. This makes authorship and mediation part of the evidence. The account is not an unedited sound recording. Nor should Wilson’s ambition to recover an unchanged earlier culture become our conclusion. A woman’s detailed recollection can preserve decisions, relationships and expertise without representing every person or directly describing the 1600 village.

deeperReading.title: Field knowledge includes boundaries and limits of memory
deeperReading.text: In her account, adjoining gardeners shared work along a boundary and sought permission before planting it. She describes resting fields flexibly, rather than following one fixed timetable. Her explanation of a garden map also names its limits: approximate positions and fields near her own family, not every garden. These statements help us ask how knowledge and use of land were negotiated. They do not create a measured survey of Big Hidatsa. The book also describes Goodbird making a model hoe under her direction from a steer shoulder blade. That identified model must not be silently equated with the separate NPS tool illustration. The modern lodge photograph and teaching-tool illustration have different limits again: they explain structures and materials without becoming dated household artifacts. A fuller account needs more women’s and families’ histories, source-specific plans and the circumstances of each later relocation.

A modern scientific graph asks a different question: when did this particular community occupy the Jean-Baptiste Lainé site? sections.title: A village joined households, fields and relationships
sections.text: The public interpretation places Wendat villages beside fields of corn, squash and beans, with farming alongside fishing, hunting, gathering, trade and diplomacy. These activities needed repeated work, stored knowledge and relationships beyond one house. House construction also required wood for frames and bark for coverings. They do not make all Iroquoian-speaking peoples one nation. Nor does the survival of a decorated pot establish the daily experience or authority of every resident.

subjects.question: What makes a promise between nations—and what would show that it was kept?
subjects.summary: Peace needed material work: protecting land, supplying goods, supporting skills and handling complaints. The Canandaigua document records commitments; Nation accounts explain speakers, wampum, cloth and continuing care. Reading these together distinguishes a promise from particular actions taken to maintain a relationship, without claiming that every commitment was fulfilled.

sections.title: A household’s food supply could become a military target
sections.text: Washington’s 31 May 1779 instructions to Sullivan targeted settlements, crops and the ability to plant again. This was an intended attack on the work sustaining communities. Bradley Powless’s Onondaga account separately describes damaged homes and food stores, displacement and the later decision to negotiate. Reading order and community account together connects diplomacy with the practical question of sustaining life. The instruction itself does not establish how much was destroyed or make every Nation’s wartime experience identical.

citations.locator: Opening orders: settlements, crops and planting

sections.title: Peace involved goods, tools and skilled work
sections.text: The treaty acknowledged particular lands and prescribed material support. Article VI described an annual allowance for clothing, domestic animals, agricultural implements and other utensils, and for skilled workers living with or near the communities. It assigned application of the allowance to a superintendent. These provisions joined farming, making and the maintenance of peace. Their wording identifies a promised arrangement and responsible role; a delivery record or account of work would be needed to investigate a particular implementation.

sections.title: Bead-making and speaking carried political knowledge
sections.text: Onondaga explains that shell pieces were shaped, smoothed and drilled to make wampum beads. Speakers connected agreements with strings or belts, and later speakers used them to remember the agreement and subsequent history. Council invitations also carried information. Making, keeping and speaking were related forms of skilled work. The Nation’s account of the Washington Belt explains its figures and longhouse through peace and friendship. That explanation comes from the account; an outside viewer cannot decode every meaning independently.

sections.title: The manuscript records more than one dated action
sections.text: The archive identifies the treaty signed 11 November 1794 and a separate U.S. ratification signed 21 January 1795. The displayed recto incorporates treaty text, names and seals within that later instrument. Its opening Washington heading therefore does not move the original negotiation into 1795. Preserving both dates lets us ask who made commitments, how they were recorded and what additional action followed. Neither the document’s formal appearance nor its seals establish that all its terms were subsequently observed.

sections.title: A continuing relationship requires particular evidence
sections.text: The Oneida Indian Nation reports recurring treaty-cloth deliveries and describes their continuing political meaning. Chief Irving Powless Jr.’s 1989 account describes another particular action: bringing wampum belts home and preparing a place for their care. These accounts concern different materials and events. They show why fulfillment cannot be reduced to signing a page. Evidence of one practice or return does not establish every land commitment, settle every dispute or erase the distinct responsibilities of the nations involved.

deeperReading.title: A return can be described by a participant
deeperReading.text: Chief Irving Powless Jr. dates his account 21 October 1989 and identifies the leaders who went to Albany to sign the return agreement. He describes arranging a table, benches and chairs in the longhouse, bringing food and receiving the belts. Care required preparation as well as a formal transfer. He also reports Chief Jake Thomas distinguishing the belts’ availability from the lengthy work of explaining them. This is a named participant’s account, not an independent inventory audit. Its practical custody passages can be discussed without reproducing the sacred songs or ceremonies also described on the public page. To trace the custody of a particular belt, a reader would also need the transfer agreement and an inventory identifying that belt.

deeperReading.title: Material evidence has a defined scope
deeperReading.text: The public Oneida account treats cloth as a symbol of a continuing government-to-government relationship and notes that individual portions have diminished. This is more specific than saying that nothing happened after the treaty, but it is narrower than an audited record of every delivery. Article VII offers another kind of question: it prescribes complaints and redress instead of private retaliation. Investigating a particular injury would require records of that complaint and response. The treaty, a Nation’s public account and a delivery receipt could therefore contribute different evidence to the same inquiry. None alone establishes complete performance or provides a present-day legal ruling.

packs.title: Connections, work and unequal power
packs.question: How did connections reshape work, belief, power and resistance?
packs.orientation: Ships joined ports through goods, money, stories and people. These connections were made by artists, translators, sailors and workers as well as rulers. Some were negotiated; others depended on conquest, enslavement and forced displacement. Begin in the 1450–1650 context, then follow selected consequences into the later eighteenth century. A companion investigation turns inland to Ottoman, Safavid and Central Asian cities and follows skilled work into later-eighteenth-century Iran.
packs.geography: Portugal, Benin, Kongo, South Asia, China, Manila, Mexico and Banda belong to different networks. The journey includes the earlier 1497–99 voyage as context and labels a Mexican jar made after 1650. Schematic routes do not establish a particular object’s itinerary. Istanbul/Iznik, Isfahan/New Julfa, Bukhara and the Shiraz political context add distinct West/Central Asian settings; a shared chapter does not merge their governments or identities. Makah Ozette, the Blackfoot hunting landscape at Head-Smashed-In and Hidatsa river villages add distinct northern histories. Southern Ontario and Canandaigua add distinct Wendat and Haudenosaunee investigations.
packs.limits: Selected African, Asian, European and American encounters, with ocean and inland investigations. This is not a complete history of Atlantic slavery, Indigenous resistance, the Indian Ocean, Ottoman Arab provinces, the wider Caucasus or Central Asia beyond the selected Bukhara case. Oceanian perspectives still need fuller treatment.

Americas.reason: Acapulco, Pacific cargoes and later Mexican ceramics; Indigenous and enslaved American experiences need fuller dossiers. Distinct Makah, Blackfoot and Hidatsa investigations add cedar work, communal hunting and village agriculture. Ozette burial estimates remain disputed; the selected hunting context is not the whole site chronology. An ancestral Wendat village and Haudenosaunee treaty diplomacy add northeastern histories. Modeled village bounds, treaty signing and U.S. ratification are different kinds of dates; no common polity or automatic succession is inferred.

Africa.reason: Expanded Benin and Kongo cases explain makers, religious translation and distinct royal evidence. Wider communities, collection histories and trafficking outcomes remain selective.

Europe.reason: Portuguese access and armed expansion; the VOC appears through Banda’s colonial records.

West/Central Asia.reason: Ottoman administration/workshops/markets, Safavid Isfahan and forced Armenian relocation, Bukhara’s urban/bookmaking contexts and later-eighteenth-century Iran now have distinct sourced dossiers. This is not an exhaustive account of Ottoman provinces, the Caucasus, pastoral societies or Central Asia.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Calicut encounter inquiry retains existing ports and intermediaries; broader Indian Ocean economies, local accounts and port histories remain selective.

East Asia.reason: Ming production and Pacific exchange; not a general survey of China, Japan or Korea.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Banda and Manila represent different roles in ocean networks. Oceania is not covered by a dossier in this pack.

investigations.title: Books, silk and power: West/Central Asia, 1500–1800
investigations.question: How did makers and urban communities work within—and beyond—courtly power?
investigations.orientation: Begin with a book likely copied and painted in different settings, then examine an Ottoman dish and emblem, an Iranian carpet and a 1789 lacquer case. Put skilled work beside patronage, markets and coercion. A luxury object cannot stand in for everyone’s experience.
investigations.geography: Distinct contexts in present-day Türkiye, Iran and Uzbekistan connect artistic production to cities, trade and political power. The manuscript’s Bukhara attribution and the carpet’s workshop location remain qualified; map points do not resolve those uncertainties.
investigations.limits: Four selected contexts within the 1500–1800 navigation frame. Their defined dates are not the lifespans of all relevant empires or peoples. The investigation includes forced Armenian relocation and urban work but cannot recover every maker, purchaser or household.

investigations.title: Makers, interpreters and unequal encounters
investigations.question: Whose knowledge made an encounter possible, and who could choose?
investigations.orientation: Compare an ocean account, an Edo carving and Kongo religious making and royal letters. The selected dates organize a thematic inquiry, not a single causal route or evidence that these particular objects and voyagers met.
investigations.geography: Approximate city and coast locators distinguish Lisbon, Malindi, Calicut, Benin City and Mbanza Kongo. No exact ship track, political border or object findspot is reconstructed.
investigations.limits: Three expansions do not complete Atlantic/Indian Ocean histories or supply independent, family or original-language acceptance.

investigations.title: Makers, patrons and markets
investigations.question: How did makers, patrons and markets organize work?
investigations.orientation: Compare a Ming jar, a Süleiman tughra and a Mughal manuscript folio. Shaping, decoration, writing and translation involved different working relationships. phases.title: Craft tasks and unpaid labor appear together
phases.text: The edition attributes Pineda’s report to [Mexico? 1619]. It identifies woodcutting, carpentry, mast-making and smithing, while reporting pay arrears and people leaving. The report covers ships, galleys and defense; it does not provide one galleon’s complete crew or prove that its wage schedules were paid.

phases.title: The selected object belongs to a later material history
phases.text: The Met dates accession 11.87.36 to approximately 1680–1700 and identifies Mexican tin-glazed earthenware. This is later than the 1595 wreck and remains distinct from imported Chinese porcelain. The catalogue does not identify its particular buyer, contents or voyage.

phases.title: A named ship’s record gives a more specific connection
phases.text: Caño Ortigosa and Lee study the Santo Cristo’s register dated at Cavite on 26 June 1726 for a voyage to Acapulco. Their discussion follows Julián Ignacio’s entry for lacquered furnishings, ceramics described as Japanese and personal belongings. The registration does not identify this Mexican jar or establish every good’s precise origin, route, sale or successful delivery.

contexts.title: Banda: trade, coercion and continuing communities

interval.label: Selected trade and displacement evidence, 1599–1630
interval.note: A selected reference around the unchanged 1621 event case, not the beginning or end of Bandanese history. The final marker is a dated colonial observation of communities in Kei, not their first existence. The separate 2019 and 2021 sources concern modern language, remembrance and public claims; they are not eyewitness accounts of 1621.

contexts.summary: Monopoly required more than a contract: control of land, food and labor changed lives. Surviving communities continued work, relationships and remembrance beyond the campaign.

phases.label: 1599: Dutch visitors enter an existing trading society
phases.title: A trading port precedes the company’s monopoly
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu describe the first Dutch visitors paying port dues and exchanging goods for nutmeg and mace. This encounter did not create Bandanese commerce or establish a monopoly in practice.

phases.label: 1609: occupation and fortification intensify conflict
phases.title: Company trading claims acquire military force
phases.text: The National Archives account places the occupation of Neira and construction of a fort in the escalation toward conquest. Treaties and company claims must be distinguished from the choices and trading practice of the communities targeted.

phases.label: 1621: removal, hunger and enslavement
phases.title: The event case examines a policy of forced displacement
phases.text: The archive presents the council’s removal decision of 24 April and Coen’s report captioned 6 May. Its account characterizes the campaign as genocide. These records expose official purposes and resistance; they do not supply the full experience of those attacked or one settled casualty count.

citations.locator: Genocide: 24 April decision; 6 May report and modern Dutch renderings

phases.label: 1622: persecution and forced work continue
phases.title: The campaign’s consequences exceed one year
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu trace renewed persecution and forced transfers after 1621. Their account connects plantation production with the cultivation and processing knowledge of enslaved Bandanese people. The 1621 case date is not an endpoint for these consequences.

phases.label: 1630: a colonial encounter records a community in Kei
phases.title: Displacement is not disappearance
phases.text: The PALA account reports that VOC visitors encountered Bandanese people in the Kei region in 1630. It also describes continuing diaspora trade and political initiatives. The record is evidence of presence at that encounter, not a precise migration route, founding date or complete family history.

contexts.title: Communal work and the later interpretation of a Blackfoot hunting landscape

interval.label: Selected later-hunting frame and later source/heritage dates, 1700–2008
interval.note: The opening retains the atlas’s selected c.1700–1850 inquiry; it does not establish the first hunt. Later phases date heritage recognition, a photograph’s publication and an archaeological book, not continued hunting through 2008. The much longer site chronology and its interruption remain distinct; seasonal tasks are not assigned invented calendar years.

contexts.summary: Preparing and coordinating a hunt, processing materials and storing food connected a cliff with camps and household work. Community-authored teaching, a modern landscape view and archaeological interpretation supply different kinds of evidence across different dates.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long site history and interruption

phases.label: c.1700: opening of the selected atlas inquiry
phases.title: A teaching boundary, not an origin
phases.text: This opening inherits the dossier’s bounded later context. UNESCO describes a much older hunting landscape with an extended interruption; no particular eighteenth-century hunt or continuous identity of all earlier users is dated here.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long chronology and interrupted hunting

phases.label: c.1850: UNESCO’s later use boundary for this site
phases.title: A site endpoint does not end a people’s knowledge
phases.text: UNESCO gives an approximate 1850 endpoint in its site-use description. The community teaching accounts explain continuing cultural knowledge; this site boundary is not the end of Blackfoot people, all bison hunting or every community’s history.

phases.label: 1981: World Heritage inscription
phases.title: Recognition is a later institutional event
phases.text: The interpretive-site history and UNESCO identify 1981 inscription. This dates heritage recognition, not construction of drive lanes or the beginning of community care for the landscape.

phases.label: 2005: publication of the landscape photograph
phases.title: A modern surface view has a particular source history
phases.text: Commons records UM’s own photograph uploaded 17 July 2005 and a public-domain dedication. The picture is a later view, not a photograph of a hunt; camera metadata is not independent verification of an exact exposure date.

phases.label: 2008: publication of Brink’s archaeological study
phases.title: An experiment tests a question about processing
phases.text: Brink’s chapter 7, printed pp. 195–198, distinguishes a modern grease-processing experiment from a recovered ancient meal. Its cattle bones and modern tools remain part of its method, rather than disappearing from the explanation.

contexts.title: Hidatsa gardens, village relocation and continuing knowledge

interval.label: Selected village, recollection and displacement records, 1600–1954
interval.note: Big Hidatsa’s original c.1600–1845 case remains exact. Later Like-a-Fishhook recollections, 1917 publication, 1953 dam completion and 1954 relocation belong to this separate reference. Different villages have distinct occupations; no continuous occupation of one place or end of Hidatsa people is implied.

contexts.summary: Women’s cultivation, houses and storage supported households and exchange. Disease, relocation and government projects changed the settings in which people carried this knowledge; later records do not become direct witnesses to every earlier village.

citations.locator: Village & Relocations; Elbowoods & Garrison Dam Relocations

phases.label: c.1600: selected Big Hidatsa occupation begins
phases.title: One village has its own frame
phases.text: NPS places establishment of Big Hidatsa around 1600. Neighboring Awatixa villages have different histories; this is not the beginning of Hidatsa people or all cultivation in the region.

phases.label: 1837: epidemic and village reorganization
phases.title: A trading region also carried danger
phases.text: MHA’s selected history describes the smallpox epidemic and subsequent consolidation of village survivors. NPS connects the epidemic with river travel. The accounts do not supply one identical household experience or a precise mortality total adopted here.

phases.label: 1845: Like-a-Fishhook established upriver
phases.title: Relocation did not end community knowledge
phases.text: MHA identifies Núeta and Hiraacá establishing Like-a-Fishhook. This changes the place of residence and the case’s village frame; it does not end gardening, family relationships or Hidatsa identity.

phases.label: 1917: publication of a woman’s mediated agricultural account
phases.title: Remembered gardens are later evidence
phases.text: The University of Minnesota book presents Maxi´diwiac’s recollections through Goodbird’s interpretation and Wilson’s editing. The foreword describes 1912 recording and later corrections. Her Like-a-Fishhook memories are not a direct transcript of earlier Big Hidatsa life.

phases.label: 1953: Garrison Dam completed, in NPS’s account
phases.title: River engineering changed the conditions of life
phases.text: The NPS account describes the dam and flooding of reservation land despite tribal objections. The construction milestone is separate from MHA’s date for completed relocation the following year.

phases.label: 1954: relocation completed, in MHA’s account
phases.title: Displacement disrupted bottomland households
phases.text: MHA describes families moved from fertile bottomlands, communities dismantled and people scattered across new tracts. Its account places relocation completion in fall 1954. These losses do not authorize a story that the communities vanished.

contexts.title: War damage, negotiation and the material work of peace

interval.label: Selected war-to-ratification frame, 1779–1795 CE
interval.note: A selected window connecting dated destructive orders, the treaty and its separate U.S. ratification. It is not the founding, ending or complete history of the Haudenosaunee. The whole 1794–1795 case interval stays unchanged. The 1989 custody account and undated present Nation accounts are later evidence clocks outside this frame.

contexts.summary: Destroying crops and homes threatened the work sustaining communities. Negotiation addressed land, peace, supplies and complaint procedures. Putting agreements into practice required further actions that the written treaty alone cannot establish.

citations.locator: Creation date and Contains: treaty and ratification

phases.label: 31 May 1779: instructions target settlements and crops
phases.title: Read an order as an intended action
phases.text: Washington instructed Sullivan to destroy settlements, ruin crops and prevent further planting. The letter establishes this program; Powless’s separate Onondaga account describes damage and displacement. The order is not itself an inventory of completed destruction.

phases.label: 11 November 1794: treaty commitments are recorded
phases.title: Peace includes land, material support and redress
phases.text: The treaty records peace and land acknowledgments, provision for continuing purchases and skilled work, and a complaint procedure. These are commitments with specified roles, rather than proof of all later conduct.

citations.locator: Articles I–III,VI,VII and dated signature block

phases.label: 21 January 1795: a separate U.S. ratification
phases.title: One archival recto carries distinct dated actions
phases.text: The archive identifies the incorporated 1794 treaty and an instrument signed by Washington and Randolph on 21 January 1795. The document’s opening heading does not move the negotiations into 1795 or make ratification evidence of complete performance.

contexts.title: Ozette: exposure, collaboration and community custody

interval.label: Selected exposure and excavation-start frame, winter 1969–70 to April 1970
interval.note: A modern research/custody frame from the Makah museum account, not a date for the houses, the whole excavation, the cultural center’s founding or the village’s life. The original disputed burial estimates remain c. 1560 or 1700, and the reported 500±50 BP is not silently converted. The c. 1910/copyright 1911 photograph is different later evidence.

contexts.summary: The museum’s account connects exposed wooden belongings with a collaboration initiated through the Tribe. Makah oral history and the decision to keep the collection on the reservation matter to how this material is interpreted.

phases.title: A bank slump exposed preserved wooden material
phases.text: MCRC describes a storm exposing belongings at the village site. A hiker contacted the Makah Tribe, and the Tribe contacted Washington State University. This modern exposure is not the ancient burial event or the beginning of Makah knowledge of the place.

phases.label: April 1970: collaborative excavation began
phases.title: Study and care followed the community’s connection to the site
phases.text: The museum dates the excavation’s start to April 1970. Its account places oral history alongside recovered evidence and states that the Tribe kept the collection on the reservation. It gives no exact museum-founding date here; that later institution is not silently assigned to April 1970.
