contexts.title: Saint-Domingue and Haiti: emancipation, work and political authority

interval.label: Selected revolutionary decisions and records,1791–1804
interval.note: A phased source inquiry, retaining the complete original case interval unchanged. The boundaries connect an uprising to independence, not the lifespan of Haitian people or a completed transition to equal land, work or political rights. Later recognition/debt and 1825 comparisons are not incorporated without separate verified sources.

contexts.summary: Resistance, provincial emancipation, military allegiances, constitutional work rules and independence were distinct changes. Their surviving records expose authority and practical stakes without recovering every cultivator’s experience or one uniform revolutionary intention.

phases.label: 1791: uprising in the northern plantation region
phases.title: Resistance did not begin everywhere in the same way
phases.text: Manigat distinguishes the northern uprising from different struggles and alliances in the West and South. Enslaved people acted within changing military and political circumstances; a later independence outcome does not prove one identical starting program.

phases.label: 1793: provincial emancipation measures
phases.title: Local struggle preceded the metropolitan decree
phases.text: The parliamentary account places Sonthonax’s northern proclamation on 29 August, followed by Polverel’s measures in other provinces. English Heritage’s brief overview instead says September for the northern measure. The discrepancy is retained in source notes; the provincial decisions are not collapsed into the separate 1794 decree.

citations.locator: Selected renewed scope; compressed northern chronology

phases.label: 1794: the French Convention decrees colonial abolition
phases.title: A rule still required political and military support
phases.text: The institutional account describes deputies from Saint-Domingue reaching the Convention and the 4 February abolition decision. A decree changes the formal legal claim; it does not itself document implementation in every place or remove the military threats that followed.

citations.locator: Le débat: delegation and Convention decision

phases.label: 1797: Louverture’s letter to Vincent
phases.title: A formerly enslaved leader defended a particular allegiance
phases.text: The catalogued 21 October letter seeks Vincent’s advocacy with the Directory, challenges racist allegations and affirms attachment to France. It is a particular leader’s argument, not proof that every formerly enslaved person agreed or that independence was already a fixed 1791 objective.

phases.label: 1801: abolition and controlled cultivation in one constitution
phases.title: Status, labor and government power were different questions
phases.text: Articles 1 and 3 retain a French connection while prohibiting slavery. Articles 14–16 insist on cultivation and authorize police regulation of cultivators’ movement. Article 28 grants Louverture life tenure. These provisions do not certify voluntary work, actual revenue shares or equal political participation.

phases.label: 1804: independence proclaimed at Gonaïves
phases.title: An official act also organized authority
phases.text: The Acte’s dateline is 1 January. Its assembled generals renounce France. The separately studied printed packet also authorizes Dessalines’s life governorship. An official declaration and a new allocation of state power do not amount to a direct record of every household’s freedom or consent.

Which records explain the work supporting city life, and whose experience remains unknown?
How can an object’s attribution be kept separate from a city’s households and political history?
How do writing and decoration connect specialized work with patrons and audiences?
How do sources reveal coercion and struggles over freedom?
How do patrons, markets and unequal power shape craft?
How do changing patrons affect books and decorative arts?
How do communities coordinate food, work and seasonal knowledge?

orientations.title: Andean makers and a Pacific encounter
orientations.question: How did skilled work continue and change within colonial relationships?

summary.title: Two different American settings
summary.text: Andean textiles and the 1595 wreck of the San Agustín at tamál-húye bring different kinds of evidence into view. Textile histories trace making across political change; Coast Miwok village archaeology investigates the use of objects from a particular maritime encounter. Neither supplies a single experience of colonization.

sections.title: Continuity did not mean unchanged circumstances
sections.text: Indigenous Andean makers continued techniques and forms while producing new combinations of motifs and commissions for churches and private patrons. The selected earlier tunic remains dated to 1450–1550. Its survival is not proof that every maker’s working conditions remained the same in the colonial period.

sections.title: An object can acquire another local use
sections.text: At Point Reyes, Asian and European materials from the wreck occur in Coast Miwok village contexts. Investigators consider how people selected and used them, rather than treating local communities as passive endpoints of a trade line. A found fragment does not by itself recover its user’s name or intention.

sections.title: Later work records need their own date
sections.text: The Manila reading’s shipbuilding reports describe early-seventeenth-century burdens on Philippine communities. They explain another part of the system, but do not identify the labour history of every person aboard the ship wrecked in 1595. The later Haitian and Canandaigua investigations likewise belong to later moments in this chapter.

orientations.scope: Selected Andean and northern Californian/Pacific settings. No common colonial experience, exact route for every object or unchanged Inka state in 1600 is inferred.
orientations.perspectives: Makers and Indigenous uses of imported material complicate elite and colonial narratives. The ship’s written record remains a mediated colonial perspective, supplemented by village archaeology.

activity.prompt: Does finding an imported fragment in a village prove that its residents used it as its makers intended?
activity.response: Describe the find context and any use traces first. Compare competing interpretations; origin establishes where it was made, not automatically how a later user understood it.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE comes shortly after the San Agustín wreck of 1595, within an expanding Pacific colonial exchange system. Andean textile work also continued under colonial conditions. The selected 1450–1550 tunic and the later shipbuilding reports remain separately dated evidence.

orientations.title: Benin and Kongo: makers, translation and power
orientations.question: How did African institutions shape objects made amid wider contacts?

summary.title: Distinct courts and religious settings
summary.text: Benin’s court-supported craft production and Kongo’s changing Christian practices were different institutional histories. An ivory saltcellar and a brass crucifix preserve decisions about form and representation. Their foreign connections do not erase the agency of African makers, patrons or interpreters.

sections.title: Making and interpreting were skilled work
sections.text: The saltcellar’s carved support joins figures and a container in ivory. Kongo translation required discussion of meanings as well as words; the selected crucifix combines a Christian subject with a particular local composition. Neither object alone establishes how every resident understood the encounter.

sections.title: Connections included unequal power
sections.text: Court patronage controlled access to skilled production. The wider histories also include coercive exchange and enslavement, rather than a story of contact as equal benefit. The linked source-qualified accounts distinguish those relationships from the limited evidence supplied by one art object.

citations.locator: 6 July and 18 October 1526: kidnapping, captives and proposed inspection

sections.title: Later texts are not evidence from the initial encounter
sections.text: Kongo’s Portuguese–Kikongo catechism of 1624 belongs well after the royal baptism of 1491 and after the 1600 snapshot. A broad sixteenth–seventeenth-century crucifix range is also not an exact production date. These clocks should remain separate.

orientations.scope: Benin and Kongo are separate selected settings, not a single African court culture or a complete account of Atlantic slavery. Broad object dates do not establish a particular transaction in 1600.
orientations.perspectives: African makers, translators and patrons appear as participants with their own institutions. Elite objects still underrepresent many households and people subjected to coercion.

activity.prompt: Why should a later bilingual religious text not be treated as a transcript of an earlier conversion?
activity.response: Keep the text’s production date, purpose and translation work separate from the earlier episode. It can reveal later interpretation and teaching without reproducing the first encounter.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE lies at the end of the selected Benin saltcellar’s approximate 1525–1600 range and within the broad date range of the Kongo crucifix. Neither is securely made in this exact year. The Kongo catechism of 1624 is a later comparison.

orientations.title: Antwerp printing and later London experiments
orientations.question: How did making and circulating records support new communities of inquiry?

summary.title: A workshop left more than finished books
summary.text: The Plantin-Moretus complex in Antwerp preserves printing equipment, a library and business archives. These different records support questions about how books were made and circulated. The firm’s late-sixteenth-century work belonged to a wider European printing landscape that included Paris and Venice.

citations.locator: Description: workshop, collections and printing centres

sections.title: A finished record depends on organized work
sections.text: Equipment and archives draw attention to production and coordination behind a printed page. The earlier Portuguese voyage reading offers a different record: a participant’s journal that later readers encounter through editing and translation. Neither a surviving press nor a printed travel account guarantees that every statement is correct.

sections.title: A later institution made checking a shared activity
sections.text: London’s Royal Society first met in 1660. Its account describes correspondence, observations, experiments and discussion, followed by publication. It also identifies early participants as exclusively male and drawn from professional and aristocratic groups. Organized inquiry was therefore a practice with restricted participation, not knowledge suddenly available on equal terms to everyone.

citations.locator: Early days: 1660 meeting, methods and membership

orientations.scope: A printing-house focus with a separately dated London comparison and an earlier travel-record destination. This is not a complete history of the Reformation, European science or all book readers.
orientations.perspectives: Workshop evidence makes production visible, while the Society’s own account identifies exclusions. Neither prominent founders nor surviving collections represent every contributor.

activity.prompt: Why does printing make a statement easier to circulate without proving it true?
activity.response: Separate production and distribution from verification. Ask who wrote the statement, what evidence supports it, how translation or editing changed it, and what another record could check.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE belongs to the continuing Plantin-Moretus publishing enterprise, after Christophe Plantin’s death in 1589. The Royal Society’s first meeting in 1660 is later; it cannot be treated as an institution already operating at this snapshot.

citations.locator: Plantin dates and firm continuation to 1867

orientations.title: Ottoman workshops, Bukhara books and a new Safavid capital
orientations.question: Which kinds of work connected institutions without sharing one ruler or one chronology?

summary.title: Several urban settings
summary.text: Ottoman production centres, Bukhara’s book and learning institutions, and Safavid Isfahan represent distinct settings. Isfahan’s late-sixteenth-century capital development took place within an older city. These histories overlap in time without forming one political system.

sections.title: Patronage depended on practical coordination
sections.text: A decorated document, a ceramic surface and a manuscript all required several tasks. Bukhara’s institutions also needed water and income; silk connected rural production with workshops and merchants. Naming a ruler or patron does not identify every maker or describe all working conditions.

sections.title: New Julfa follows forced relocation
sections.text: Isfahan’s New Julfa history belongs to the forced movement of Armenian communities in the early seventeenth century. Commercial success in the later quarter cannot erase that coercion, and the quarter cannot be projected into the 1600 snapshot simply because Isfahan was already a capital.

orientations.scope: Selected Ottoman, Central Asian and Safavid urban histories. No uniform workshop, seamless trade route or exact political border is inferred; later Zand evidence belongs to another phase.
orientations.perspectives: Documents and commissions foreground patrons; water systems, material tasks and displacement add other relationships. Many workers’ names and experiences remain unrecorded.

activity.prompt: Can a prosperous later trading quarter be used to describe the city before its inhabitants were relocated there?
activity.response: State the relocation and settlement dates first. Explain the later commercial institutions without backdating them or treating eventual prosperity as proof of voluntary migration.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE follows Isfahan’s capital transfer of 1597–98 and overlaps selected Ottoman and Bukhara institutional histories. New Julfa’s early-seventeenth-century forced relocation and later merchant networks come afterward; they do not describe the quarter in 1600.

orientations.title: Mughal books, court residences and commercial connections
orientations.question: How did a manuscript connect skilled people across languages and places?

summary.title: Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore and a wider economy
summary.text: Akbar’s reign, 1556–1605, included a courtly manuscript workshop associated first with Fatehpur Sikri and then Lahore. Gujarat’s commercial centres added another setting within Mughal expansion. Court production was connected with a wider economy, without representing every household or region.

citations.locator: Akbar, Gujarat and royal atelier paragraphs

sections.title: A book was a collaborative object
sections.text: Painters, calligraphers, illuminators and binders performed distinct work. Translation made Sanskrit narratives available in Persian, while surviving records sometimes name contributors. A painting’s subject is not a record of a historical event, and a name attached to one manuscript cannot supply the maker of another.

sections.title: The court moved; the evidence has several dates
sections.text: Fatehpur Sikri’s main building programme preceded the move to Lahore in 1585 described by the museum. The selected manuscript page has its own catalogue range. A reign, a court residence, a translation project and a surviving copy therefore cannot share a single automatic date.

orientations.scope: A justified focus on court book production across named residences, with Gujarat as a commercial context. It does not establish an agrarian census, universal literacy or the experience of every South Asian community.
orientations.perspectives: Named contributors help reveal collaboration beside royal patronage. Sources remain strongest for elite commissions and weaker for most producers and readers outside the court.

activity.prompt: Why should a translated story, its illustrated copy and a ruler’s reign receive separate dates?
activity.response: Identify the event or process each date describes. Translation, copying and illustration can happen at different times, and a reign only supplies an outer political frame.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE falls near the end of Akbar’s reign of 1556–1605. The workshop history includes earlier work at Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore, but the selected page must retain its own catalogue range. Neither residence nor every illustrated book is dated simply by the reign.

orientations.title: Ming workshops and Momoyama Japan
orientations.question: How did objects express authority while their makers worked within different institutions?

summary.title: Separate production settings
summary.text: Ming ceramic production involved court orders as well as other buyers. In Japan, the Momoyama account connects decorated castles and objects with competing warlords and changing power. These were distinct settings, not one East Asian style or shared government.

sections.title: A design still needed material work
sections.text: The selected Ming jar combines decoration below and above the glaze. Shaping, firing and surface work required coordinated skill. Japanese castle decoration and furnishings expressed another relationship between patrons and makers; visual splendour alone does not tell us the worker’s freedom or income.

sections.title: War and exchange were not opposites
sections.text: The museum’s Momoyama account describes continuing connections with China and Korea alongside Hideyoshi’s destructive invasions of Korea. It is therefore misleading to tell the period only through imported goods or artistic achievement. Later Tokugawa and Qing settings belong to subsequent political phases, not an unchanging 1600 map.

citations.locator: Final paragraph: invasions and overseas contacts

orientations.scope: Selected Chinese and Japanese production/patronage settings. The museum’s art-period convention 1573–1615 does not define every political transition; no total-isolation claim or uniformly beneficial exchange is adopted.
orientations.perspectives: Court and elite collections favour commissioned objects. The account keeps destructive war visible and does not infer ordinary experience from luxury surfaces.

activity.prompt: Why should an account of artistic exchange also examine war and coercion?
activity.response: Ask how people, materials and techniques moved, and who bore the costs. A beautiful object does not establish voluntary movement or benefit for all participants.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE falls within Ming rule and the museum’s Momoyama art-period frame in Japan. The selected Ming object has its own date; later Qing and Tokugawa institutions should not be imported into the snapshot as though their full later arrangements already existed.

orientations.title: Banda and Manila: exchange, provision and coercion
orientations.question: When does a trading relationship become an attempt to control people and food?

summary.title: Two maritime settings
summary.text: Banda’s spice exchange connected island production with imported food. The Manila system linked Philippine and American settings through Pacific voyages. These networks involved different local communities and institutions; a map of moving goods cannot by itself explain their working conditions.

sections.title: The first visit was not the later conquest
sections.text: The Westfries Museum account dates the first Dutch visit to Banda to 1599, before the VOC existed. It describes purchases and port fees before later treaty claims and violence. Keeping that sequence visible prevents the events of 1621 from replacing the islands’ earlier social and commercial history.

citations.locator: Opening 1599 visit; 1602 alliance and later escalation

sections.title: Control over trade could become control over survival
sections.text: The archive explains why restricting exchange endangered Banda’s food supply. Its 1621 records concern removal, destruction and coercion. The Manila shipbuilding accounts separately describe burdens on Philippine communities. Neither should be turned into a neutral story of efficient global connection.

sections.title: A Pacific comparison needs its own record
sections.text: The 1595 San Agustín wreck in Coast Miwok territory supplies a particular Pacific encounter. It is not evidence of a Banda–California voyage or a history of all Oceanian islands. The two maritime inquiries remain separate even when they share questions about provisions and work.

orientations.scope: Banda and the Philippine–American Pacific system, with no invented continuous route between them. The reading does not claim coverage of every Oceanian society or backdate VOC conquest to 1600.
orientations.perspectives: Colonial records dominate the archive and are read for their perspective. Bandanese communities and Philippine workers appear through different, uneven records rather than as anonymous cargo-route endpoints.

activity.prompt: Why is it misleading to label a 1599 encounter as the 1621 conquest?
activity.response: Keep initial purchases, subsequent coercive claims and the later conquest separately dated. Explain change over time without assuming that the first encounter already contained every later institution.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE follows the first Dutch visit to Banda in 1599 and the San Agustín wreck in 1595. The VOC’s later creation and Banda conquest of 1621 have not yet occurred. This earlier exchange setting is independently described rather than produced by extending the 1621 case backward.
